name: Short-duration high yield investing
heading: The Structural Opportunity: Earning High Yield Credit Spreads
caseLead: High-yield corporate bonds offer additional income over government bonds to compensate for default risk, and this spread has historically exceeded realised credit losses. The premium persists because many pension funds and insurers are restricted from holding lower-rated bonds, so borrowers must offer higher yields to attract other buyers, while short maturities limit the loss from higher interest rates and give the investor frequent chances to reassess credit quality.
caseRest: The main risk is credit losses, which rise when economic growth slows or financing becomes more expensive, so defaults can increase within months. Short maturities limit the effect of interest rate changes but do not reduce the risk of default, and bond prices can fall sharply when investors sell in a weak market. The headline yield can therefore understate the downside risk, as losses on lower-rated bonds can equal a year or more of coupon income, as in 2008 and March 2020.
figNote: The large figure on each card shows the widest level reached by the US high-yield credit spread during the episode, in basis points, where 100 basis points equal one percentage point. The spread is the extra yield that high-yield bonds pay over US Treasuries, so a higher figure means investors demanded more compensation for default risk.

events.title: Euro crisis widens high-yield spreads
events.text: Fears that Greece would default and the crisis would spread to Italy and Spain widened the US high-yield spread to about 880 basis points in early October 2011. The strategy lost because bond prices fell by more than the coupons earned in the period.

events.title: Oil price collapse raises default fears
events.text: Brent crude near 28 dollars threatened defaults among US energy producers and lifted the US high-yield spread to about 890 basis points in February 2016. The strategy lost because energy bonds, about 14% of the market, fell sharply despite short maturities.

events.title: Rate rises and falling oil widen spreads
events.text: Federal Reserve rate rises, a 40% fall in oil prices from October and falling equity prices widened the US high-yield spread to about 530 basis points in December 2018. Results were mixed because short maturities limited price losses, but energy bonds still lost value.

events.title: Covid triples the high-yield credit spread
events.text: The US high-yield spread rose from about 360 basis points in February to 1,090 on 23 March 2020 as lockdowns and a fall in oil prices raised default fears. The strategy lost because bond liquidity fell and even short-dated bonds declined in price.

events.title: Rising rates and war lift borrowing costs
events.text: The Federal Reserve's rate rises and the war in Ukraine lifted the US high-yield spread to about 600 basis points in July 2022. Results were mixed because short maturities limited losses from higher Treasury yields, but wider spreads still reduced bond prices.

events.title: Tariff announcement briefly widens spreads
events.text: US tariff announcements widened the US high-yield spread to about 460 basis points on 7 April 2025, before it fell back within weeks as tariffs were paused. The strategy gained because short-dated bonds lost little and coupons continued to accrue.

instrument: US and European high-yield bonds; up to three years to maturity; rebalanced monthly
rules: Bonds rated BB to B with at most three years to maturity; energy issuers capped at 10%; exposure reduced when the spread widens by 150 basis points in a month
costs: Estimated bid-ask spreads, commissions and fund fees deducted at each monthly rebalance

entry: Bond yield at least 3 percentage points above Treasuries of the same maturity
size: Set to a 5.5% annualised volatility target
exit: Bonds sold when maturity falls below 6 months or the rating is cut
stop: Exposure halved if the high-yield spread widens by 150 basis points in a month
marketWatch: The high-yield credit spread, the rate of corporate defaults and lender surveys on credit standards are the main indicators for this strategy. Rehyn tracks energy prices and central bank policy because they affect borrowing costs and cash flow for lower-rated companies. A rise in refinancing needs in the coming year matters because it raises the share of companies that cannot refinance on current terms.

favourable.heading: Low defaults and narrow spreads
favourable.text: Steady growth favours the strategy because defaults stay low and coupons accumulate without price losses. In 2013 and 2014, the US high-yield default rate stayed below 3% and the strategy earned most of its return from coupons.

favourable.heading: Rising rates with short maturities
favourable.text: Rising interest rates favour the strategy compared with long-dated bonds because short maturities lose little price and the portfolio reinvests at higher coupons. In 2022, US high-yield bonds with maturities under three years lost less than half as much as the broader high-yield market.

favourable.heading: Fast recoveries after credit scares
favourable.text: Quick recoveries favour the strategy because bonds that mature within three years return to par before default risk materialises. After the March 2020 sell-off, the Federal Reserve's purchases of corporate bonds helped narrow the spread from 1,090 to about 500 basis points by August.

adverse.heading: Recession and rising defaults
adverse.text: A recession hurts the strategy because lower-rated companies lose revenue, default more often and repay less on their bonds. In 2009, the US high-yield default rate peaked above 10%, so coupon income was not enough to offset losses on bonds issued by weaker borrowers.

adverse.heading: Commodity price collapse
adverse.text: A fall in commodity prices hurts the strategy because energy and mining companies make up a large share of high-yield issuers. Brent fell from about 115 dollars in mid-2014 to about 28 dollars in January 2016, energy defaults rose sharply and the spread widened to 890 basis points.

adverse.heading: Credit market liquidity stress
adverse.text: A loss of market liquidity hurts the strategy because investors can sell bonds only at large discounts, even if the bonds mature soon. In March 2020, the high-yield spread rose by about 700 basis points in a month as bid-ask spreads on corporate bonds widened sharply.

infoHist: Historical results show the strategy's peak-to-trough drawdown during each event, measured from its value just before the event to its lowest point using the default backtest parameters above. Each event window runs from the last market high before the shock to the market low.
infoForward: Scenario results show the estimated profit or loss over the first month of each scenario. Rehyn's scenario engine projects moves in credit spreads, default rates and Treasury yields, which are then applied to the strategy's current holdings, including the credit protection.
